## Purpose

This procedure describes the determination of alkalinity in water
samples by potentiometric titration with standardized sulfuric acid,
following Standard Methods 2320 B [@apha2012]. Alkalinity is the
acid-neutralizing capacity of water and is primarily a function of
carbonate, bicarbonate, and hydroxide content. It is a fundamental
parameter for characterizing water chemistry, assessing buffering
capacity, and interpreting corrosivity, hardness, and suitability for
irrigation or aquatic life.

## Scope

- **Applies to:** Surface water, groundwater, stormwater, and wastewater
  samples collected per
  [SOP-F300](../field_sops/SOP-F300-surface-water-sampling.qmd)
- **Does not apply to:** Soil alkalinity, industrial process water
  requiring specialized titration protocols, or samples with alkalinity
  above 500 mg/L as CaCO~3~ (which require 0.1 N titrant; see note in
  Section 6.4)
- **Location:** EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

## Definitions

- **Acid-neutralizing capacity (ANC):** The capacity of a water to
  neutralize strong acid; for most natural waters, ANC is
  approximately equal to total alkalinity.
- **Alkalinity:** The capacity of water to resist acidification,
  expressed in mg/L as CaCO~3~; in natural waters, primarily
  contributed by bicarbonate (HCO~3~^-^), carbonate (CO~3~^2-^), and
  hydroxide (OH^-^).
- **Bicarbonate alkalinity:** Alkalinity attributable to HCO~3~^-^;
  the dominant form in most fresh waters at pH 6.3--10.3.
- **Endpoint pH:** The pH at which the titration is stopped to
  correspond to the equivalence point of the reaction between the
  alkalinity species and the standard acid; 4.5 for routine total
  alkalinity, 8.3 for phenolphthalein (P) alkalinity.
- **Normality (N):** The number of gram-equivalents of a substance per
  liter of solution; for H~2~SO~4~ used in alkalinity titrations, 1 N
  = 0.5 M because each H~2~SO~4~ donates 2 protons.
- **Phenolphthalein alkalinity (P alkalinity):** Alkalinity measured
  to the pH 8.3 endpoint; represents OH^-^ and half of CO~3~^2-^
  content; zero if the sample pH is initially below 8.3.
- **Potentiometric titration:** Titration in which the endpoint is
  determined by monitoring electrode potential (pH) rather than by a
  color indicator.
- **Standardization:** The process of determining the exact
  concentration of a titrant by titrating a primary standard of known
  purity and mass (e.g., anhydrous Na~2~CO~3~).
- **Total alkalinity (T alkalinity):** Alkalinity measured to the pH
  4.3--4.5 endpoint; represents the sum of all alkalinity species.

| Role              | Responsibility                                     |
|:------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|
| Lab PI            | Approve SOP, ensure training compliance            |
| Lab Manager       | Prepare and standardize titrant, maintain pH meter |
| Trained Personnel | Perform titrations, record and report results      |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent use           |

## Safety and Hazards

::: callout-warning
### Hazards

- **Chemical:** Sulfuric acid (0.02 N) is a dilute acid but can cause
  skin and eye irritation. Concentrated H~2~SO~4~ used to prepare stock
  solutions is severely corrosive.
- **Physical:** Glassware (burets, beakers) poses a breakage and
  laceration risk.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Safety glasses
- [ ] Lab coat
- [ ] Nitrile gloves

### Emergency Procedures

For acid splashes to skin or eyes, flush immediately with water at the
eyewash station for at least 15 minutes. For concentrated acid spills,
neutralize with sodium bicarbonate and refer to [SOP-L003 Hazardous
Materials Handling](SOP-L003-hazardous-materials-handling.qmd).

## Equipment and Materials

### Equipment

| Item | Notes |
|:-----------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| pH meter with combination electrode | Calibrated per [SOP-L300](SOP-L300-pH-conductivity-bench.qmd) |
| Magnetic stir plate and stir bar | For continuous mixing during titration |
| Buret, 50 mL (Class A) | For samples with alkalinity above 20 mg/L as CaCO~3~ |
| Buret, 10 mL (Class A, microburet) | For low-alkalinity samples (below 20 mg/L) |
| Buret stand and clamp | -- |
| Volumetric flasks (100 mL, 1 L) | For standard preparation |
| Graduated cylinder (100 mL) | For measuring sample volumes |
| Beakers (150 -- 250 mL) | For titration |
| Analytical balance | 0.1 mg readability; see [SOP-L200](SOP-L200-analytical-balance-calibration.qmd) |

### Reagents

| Item | Notes |
|:-----------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Standard H~2~SO~4~, 0.1 N | Prepare from concentrated H~2~SO~4~ or purchase pre-made; standardize against Na~2~CO~3~ (see Section 6.1) |
| Standard H~2~SO~4~, 0.02 N | Dilute from 0.1 N stock (see Section 6.2) |
| Sodium carbonate (Na~2~CO~3~), primary standard grade | For standardizing the acid titrant |
| pH buffer solutions (pH 4.01, 7.00, 10.01) | For pH meter calibration |
| Deionized water (Type I or II) | For reagent preparation, blanks, and rinsing |

### Optional Indicator Solutions

Color indicators may be used for preliminary or routine titrations when
the sample is free of interfering color and turbidity. Potentiometric
(pH meter) titration is preferred for accuracy.

| Indicator | Endpoint pH | Application |
|:------------------------------|:----------------|:------------------------|
| Phenolphthalein | 8.3 | Phenolphthalein (P) alkalinity |
| Bromcresol green | 4.5 | Total (T) alkalinity |
| Mixed bromcresol green -- methyl red | 4.5 | Total (T) alkalinity |

## Procedure

### Standardizing the 0.1 N H~2~SO~4~

1.  Dry 3--5 g of primary standard Na~2~CO~3~ at 250 C for 4 hours and
    cool in a desiccator
2.  Weigh 2.500 +/- 0.200 g (to the nearest 0.001 g) into a 1 L
    volumetric flask. Dissolve in DI water and bring to volume. This
    produces an approximately 0.05 N Na~2~CO~3~ solution.
3.  Pipette 40.00 mL of the Na~2~CO~3~ solution into a 250 mL beaker.
    Add approximately 60 mL of DI water.
4.  Titrate potentiometrically with the approximately 0.1 N H~2~SO~4~ to
    a pH of about 5
5.  Remove the electrodes, rinse into the beaker, and gently boil the
    solution for 3--5 minutes under a watch glass to expel CO~2~
6.  Cool to room temperature, rinse the watch glass into the beaker, and
    continue titrating to the pH inflection point
7.  Calculate the normality of the acid:

$$N_{\text{acid}} = \frac{A \times B}{53.00 \times C}$$

where $A$ = g Na~2~CO~3~ weighed into the 1 L flask, $B$ = mL Na~2~CO~3~
solution taken for titration, and $C$ = mL acid used.

8.  Adjust to 0.1000 N or use the measured normality in all subsequent
    calculations. At 0.1000 N, 1.00 mL = 5.00 mg CaCO~3~.

### Preparing the 0.02 N H~2~SO~4~ Working Titrant

1.  Dilute 200.00 mL of standardized 0.1000 N H~2~SO~4~ to 1000 mL with
    DI water in a volumetric flask
2.  Mix thoroughly
3.  Verify the normality by titrating 15.00 mL of 0.05 N Na~2~CO~3~ as
    described in Section 6.1
4.  At 0.02 N, 1.00 mL = 1.00 mg CaCO~3~
5.  Store in a tightly capped borosilicate glass or polyethylene bottle.
    Do not keep for longer than 1 week without re-standardization.

### Sample Collection and Handling

1.  Collect samples in polyethylene or borosilicate glass bottles per
    [SOP-F300](../field_sops/SOP-F300-surface-water-sampling.qmd)
2.  Fill sample bottles completely with no headspace; CO~2~ exchange
    with air will alter the alkalinity
3.  Analyze samples as soon as possible after collection, ideally within
    24 hours. Refrigerate at 4 C if analysis must be delayed.
4.  Do not filter, dilute, concentrate, or otherwise alter the sample
    before titration

### Selecting Sample Size and Titrant

Choose the sample volume and titrant normality to use a reasonable
volume of titrant (ideally 20 mL or more from a 50 mL buret) for good
volumetric precision:

| Expected Alkalinity (mg/L as CaCO~3~) | Sample Volume | Titrant Normality |
|:------------------------------------|:----------------|:-----------------|
| Less than 20 | 200 mL | 0.02 N (10 mL microburet) |
| 20 -- 100 | 100 mL | 0.02 N |
| 100 -- 500 | 100 mL | 0.1 N |

If the expected alkalinity is unknown, perform a preliminary titration
with indicator to estimate the range before running the potentiometric
titration.

### pH Meter Calibration

Calibrate the pH meter with a three-point calibration (pH 4.01, 7.00,
10.01) per [SOP-L300](SOP-L300-pH-conductivity-bench.qmd) before each
titration session. Verify that the calibration slope is between 90% and
102% of theoretical.

### Potentiometric Titration

1.  Measure the selected sample volume (e.g., 100 mL) into a clean
    beaker using a graduated cylinder
2.  Place the beaker on the magnetic stir plate and add a clean stir
    bar. Set the stirrer to a speed that produces a gentle vortex
    without splashing or entraining air.
3.  Immerse the pH electrode in the sample. Record the initial pH.
4.  Fill the buret with standardized H~2~SO~4~ (0.02 N or 0.1 N as
    selected in Section 6.4). Record the initial buret reading.
5.  **Phenolphthalein alkalinity (P):** If the initial pH is above 8.3,
    titrate to pH 8.3, recording the volume of acid used. This is the P
    alkalinity endpoint.
6.  **Total alkalinity (T):** Continue titrating to the total alkalinity
    endpoint. Select the endpoint pH from the table below based on the
    expected alkalinity concentration:

| Total Alkalinity (mg/L as CaCO~3~) | Endpoint pH |
|:-----------------------------------|:------------|
| Approximately 30                   | 4.9         |
| Approximately 150                  | 4.6         |
| Approximately 500                  | 4.3         |
| Routine or automated analyses      | 4.5         |

7.  As the endpoint is approached, add acid in smaller increments
    (0.1--0.2 mL) and allow pH equilibrium to be reached before adding
    more titrant
8.  Record the final buret reading

::: callout-tip
### Tip

For best results, record the pH after each addition of acid and
construct a full titration curve. The inflection point (steepest slope)
on the curve confirms the endpoint pH. This is especially important for
samples with unusual chemistry (e.g., high phosphate or silicate
content) where the standard endpoint pH may not correspond to the true
equivalence point.
:::

### Low-Alkalinity Method (Below 20 mg/L as CaCO~3~)

For samples with alkalinity below 20 mg/L, use a 200 mL sample volume
and titrate with 0.02 N H~2~SO~4~ from a 10 mL microburet. Record
intermediate pH values to construct a titration curve and determine the
endpoint from the inflection point. Report only low-alkalinity values
determined by this method.

## Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

### Calculations

**Total alkalinity** (mg/L as CaCO~3~):

$$\text{Alkalinity} = \frac{A \times N \times 50{,}000}{V}$$

where $A$ = mL of standard acid used, $N$ = normality of the acid, and
$V$ = mL of sample.

**Phenolphthalein alkalinity** uses the same formula but substitutes the
volume of acid titrated to pH 8.3.

### Alkalinity Species

Once P and T alkalinity are determined, the individual carbonate species
can be calculated:

| Condition | Hydroxide (OH^-^) | Carbonate (CO~3~^2-^) | Bicarbonate (HCO~3~^-^) |
|:----------------|:----------------|:------------------|:--------------------|
| P = 0     | 0                 | 0                     | T                       |
| P \< T/2  | 0                 | 2P                    | T -- 2P                 |
| P = T/2   | 0                 | 2P                    | 0                       |
| P \> T/2  | 2P -- T           | 2(T -- P)             | 0                       |
| P = T     | T                 | 0                     | 0                       |

All values are expressed as mg/L CaCO~3~.

### QC Requirements

- Standardize titrant before each batch and at least weekly
- Run a DI water blank at the start of each session; the blank should
  consume less than 0.2 mL of 0.02 N acid
- Prepare and titrate a laboratory fortified blank (LFB) using a known
  concentration of Na~2~CO~3~ at least once per batch of 20 samples.
  Recovery should be 90--110%.
- Run duplicate titrations on at least 10% of samples. Acceptable
  precision: +/- 5% relative percent difference for samples above 20
  mg/L as CaCO~3~.
- Record all QC results in the laboratory notebook

## Waste Disposal

| Waste Type | Disposal Method |
|:------------------------------|:----------------------------------------|
| Titrated samples (no hazardous additions) | Drain with copious water |
| Spent acid titrant | Neutralize with sodium bicarbonate to pH 6--8, then drain |
| Na~2~CO~3~ standardization waste | Drain with copious water |
| Used pH buffer solutions | Collect in waste container per [SOP-L300](SOP-L300-pH-conductivity-bench.qmd) |

## Training Record

Before performing alkalinity titrations independently, personnel must:

1.  Read this SOP in full
2.  Complete [SOP-L002 Laboratory
    Safety](SOP-L002-laboratory-safety.qmd) and [SOP-L300 pH and
    Conductivity](SOP-L300-pH-conductivity-bench.qmd) training
3.  Demonstrate pH meter calibration with acceptable slope
4.  Prepare and standardize a batch of H~2~SO~4~ titrant under
    supervision with normality within 2% of the target value
5.  Perform at least three practice titrations on known standards with
    acceptable recovery (90--110%)
6.  Be signed off by the PI or lab manager

## Appendix A: Titrant Preparation Quick Reference {.appendix}

### N H~2~SO~4~ from Concentrated H~2~SO~4~

Concentrated H~2~SO~4~ is approximately 36 N.

1.  Add approximately 900 mL of DI water to a 1 L volumetric flask
2.  Slowly add 2.8 mL of concentrated H~2~SO~4~ to the water (**always
    add acid to water**)
3.  Mix, cool to room temperature, and bring to volume with DI water
4.  Standardize against primary standard Na~2~CO~3~ (Section 6.1)

### N H~2~SO~4~ from 0.1 N Stock

1.  Transfer 200.00 mL of standardized 0.1000 N H~2~SO~4~ to a 1 L
    volumetric flask
2.  Bring to volume with DI water and mix thoroughly

## Appendix B: Example Calculation {.appendix}

```{r}
#| label: alkalinity-calc
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Alkalinity calculation per Standard Methods 2320 B
acid_mL <- 24.5          # mL of standard acid used
acid_N <- 0.02           # Normality of acid (eq/L)
sample_mL <- 100         # mL of sample titrated

alkalinity_mg_L <- (acid_mL * acid_N * 50000) / sample_mL

cat(sprintf("Total alkalinity: %.1f mg/L as CaCO3\n", alkalinity_mg_L))
```

## Appendix C: Troubleshooting {.appendix}

| Symptom | Probable Cause | Corrective Action |
|:----------------------|:------------------------|:-----------------------|
| Endpoint difficult to identify | Low alkalinity; flat titration curve | Use 200 mL sample, 0.02 N acid, microburet; construct full titration curve |
| Blank consumes excessive acid | CO~2~ absorbed into DI water; contaminated glassware | Use freshly boiled and cooled DI water; acid-wash glassware |
| Duplicate precision exceeds 5% RPD | Inconsistent titrant delivery; pH meter drift | Check buret for air bubbles; recalibrate pH meter; ensure pH equilibrium at endpoint |
| Alkalinity result seems too high | Sample exposed to air (CO~2~ loss raised pH) | Analyze samples promptly; fill bottles with no headspace |
| Alkalinity result seems too low | CO~2~ absorbed during storage or titration | Minimize exposure to air; do not stir vigorously enough to entrain air |
